phonemes.desc: Long diphthong αι [ai̯] with acute pitch accent; the alpha is open and the iota forms an off-glide.
Short [da], the middle syllable of the name.
Short [los], the final syllable with a clear liquid l.

pronunciation.approximation: 'DIE-dah-los' — the first syllable is long and carries the ancient pitch rise; the remaining syllables are short and light.

pronunciation.note: The Greek Δαίδαλος contains both stress (acute on the diphthong) and length (the diphthong αι is long), making it a Tier 1 restoration. The Latin-derived English form Daedalus is a secondary spelling that preserves the consonants but obscures the original Greek vowel quantities.

domains.title: The Cunning Craftsman
domains.subtitle: Inventor, Architect, and Wingsmith
domains.lead: Daidalos is the master craftsman of Greek mythology: the architect of the Labyrinth, the maker of moving statues, and the father of Icarus. His name means "cunningly wrought" and became a byword for any work so skillful that it seemed alive. He is the first engineer in Western literature, the inventor whose ingenuity saves him and destroys those he loves.

mythology.lead: The myths of Daidalos are preserved in Homer, the lost *Catalogue of Women*, Diodorus Siculus, Ovid, and Apollodorus. They celebrate the power of human invention and warn against its costs: jealousy, exile, and the death of a son.

myths.title: The Killing of Talos
myths.text: Daidalos was born in Athens, where his skill as an inventor aroused the jealousy of his nephew Talos (or Perdix). When the boy invented the saw and the potter's wheel, Daidalos threw him from the Acropolis in envy. For this murder he was exiled from Athens and fled to Crete, where King Minos welcomed him.

myths.title: The Labyrinth
myths.text: At Knossos, Daidalos built the Labyrinth to house the Minotaur, the half-man, half-bull born of Pasiphae. The maze was so cunningly designed that even its maker could barely find his way out. When Theseus came to slay the Minotaur, Ariadne gave him the thread that Daidalos had taught her to use.

myths.title: The Wings
myths.text: When Minos imprisoned Daidalos and his son Icarus in the Labyrinth, Daidalos made wings from feathers and wax. He warned Icarus not to fly too close to the sun, but the boy, exulting in flight, ignored him. The wax melted, Icarus fell into the sea, and Daidalos flew on alone to Sicily.

myths.title: Death of Daidalos
myths.text: In Sicily, Daidalos built marvellous works for King Cocalus. When Minos came to demand his surrender, Cocalus' daughters killed Minos in his bath. Daidalos lived out his life in Sicily, still inventing, still exiled from the ordinary happiness of family and home.

syncretism: The Greek Daidalos was absorbed into Roman literature as Daedalus, most famously in Ovid's *Metamorphoses*. In the Renaissance he became an emblem of the artist as rebel and genius, and in modern culture he stands for every inventor who creates what he cannot control. James Joyce made Stephen Dedalus a Daidalos-figure, the young artist escaping the nets of family, religion, and nation. The name has also been used for spacecraft, engineering projects, and artificial-intelligence ventures.
culturalLegacy: Daidalos is the archetype of the engineer, the artist, and the scientist whose creations escape his intentions. He built the Labyrinth, the wings, and the moving statues; each invention brought wonder and disaster. Modern discussions of artificial intelligence, genetic engineering, and autonomous weapons revisit his dilemma: can we make things so complex that even their makers cannot predict their effects? Daidalos reminds us that skill without wisdom is exile.
extendedMeditation:
Daidalos is the first Western portrait of the inventor as tragic hero. His gifts are extraordinary; his judgement is not. He kills his nephew from envy, builds a prison for a monster, and loses his son to the very technology that saved him. Each invention solves one problem and creates another.

To meditate on Daidalos is to meditate on the double edge of human making. We are the species that makes wings, and we are the species whose children fly too high. The question is not whether to invent but whether we can invent with the humility that knows our limits.
originalScriptNote: The name is written in Greek as Δαίδαλος. The first syllable is a long diphthong αι with an acute accent. The plain ASCII daedalus flattens the diphthong into ae and removes the accent. The PuniCodex restoration Daidalos preserves the scholarly transliteration of the Greek form and is classified as Tier 1 because the diphthong is long and accented.
